content: Mahadevan and Vogel (2018) utilized a combination of grey literature and interviews with key informants to identify barriers and facilitators to the implementation of home-based records. They also examined values, resources, equity, acceptability, and feasibility associated with these records. The methods for identifying grey literature, conducting interviews, and applying a matrix-based analytical framework are detailed in the final report available from the WHO Department of Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the effects of home-based records on priority health outcomes. The inclusion criteria were based on population, intervention, comparator, and outcome (PICO) questions. Thirteen studies were included in the review: nine randomized controlled trials (RCTs), one cluster RCT, a three-year follow-up RCT, and two non-randomized controlled studies. These studies were conducted in high-income countries such as Australia, England, Norway, and the USA, as well as in lowand middle-income countries like Cambodia, Indonesia, Mongolia, and Pakistan. Participants included pregnant or postpartum women, infants, children attending immunization clinics, and children with disabilities. The types of home-based records studied included pregnancy or maternity health records, maternal and child health (MCH) handbooks, child health records, vaccination-only records, and combined child health, vaccination, growth, and development records. No studies compared the intensity of use of these records. In one cluster RCT by Osaki et al. (2018), the MCH handbook was sporadically available in control areas, potentially causing contamination and reducing observed effects. Despite this, the study was retained for comparison of use versus non-use of home-based records, as there was no coordinated effort to use records in the control areas. Eighteen documents describing the implementation of home-based records were reviewed, including technical briefs, reports, presentations, a case study, a blog post, a working paper, a newspaper article, and a project proposal. These documents covered implementation in lowand middle-income countries such as Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Cameroon, Ethiopia, Ghana, India, Jordan, Kenya, Liberia, Madagascar, Nepal, Pakistan, and Vietnam. Three documents addressed implementation across multiple countries in Africa and Asia. Additionally, 13 key informants were interviewed, including individuals associated with JICA, John Snow, Inc., UNRWA, and UNFPA, who provided insights into the implementation of home-based records. Interviews were conducted via phone or Skype. No studies meeting the inclusion criteria were found in the review of cost-effectiveness and economic evaluations. A cost analysis was conducted using average costs provided by JICA for home-based records in Burundi, Indonesia, and Vietnam. Costing items included design, printing, distribution, orientation, training, monitoring, supervision, evaluation, scale-up, and routine maintenance. Printing costs for various types of home-based records were also provided. However, the cost-estimate exercise was limited, as unit costs could not be determined, and the results were not generalizable beyond the countries studied. The effects of home-based records on maternal, newborn, and child health (MNCH) outcomes were evaluated. For maternal outcomes, no significant effect was observed on antenatal visits, though there was increased care-seeking for pregnancy complications in intervention areas compared to control areas, albeit not statistically significant. More women in intervention areas reported receiving two doses of tetanus immunization during pregnancy compared to control groups. Slightly more women in intervention areas reported professional childbirth care, but the difference was not significant. There was a small reduction in smoking behavior among household members of women receiving the MCH handbook. Only one of six behaviors related to husbands' support for birth preparation showed a significant effect (saving money for childbirth). For newborn outcomes, there was increased care-seeking for newborn complications in intervention areas, though not statistically significant. Slight improvements in breastfeeding initiation were observed among women with access to an MCH handbook, but the difference was not significant. One of three behaviors related to husbands' support for newborn care showed a significant effect (keeping the infant warm). There was a small but non-significant difference in APGAR scores with the use of MCH handbooks. Women using the MCH handbook were less likely to report exclusive breastfeeding for six months compared to the control group, though the difference was not significant. However, women in the MCH handbook group were more likely to practice complementary feeding after six months and continue breastfeeding up to 23 months. Respondents in intervention areas were more likely to ensure children received Vitamin A supplements and provide home care for children with coughs. For child outcomes, fewer underweight children and moderately fewer children with stunted growth were observed in intervention areas compared to control areas, with the latter reaching statistical significance. There was a moderate reduction in the risk of cognitive delay in the group receiving the MCH handbook versus the control group at a three-year follow-up. The review also highlighted privacy concerns related to HIV information in home-based records and electronic health records, as well as concerns about over-diagnosis by providers in certain settings. Women and caregivers valued home-based records, with some reporting that the records demonstrated their awareness of health and increased attention from providers. However, the extent to which loss of records posed a challenge varied among respondents.
